newsitem.title: USA: Beepers go awry across U.S. for half-hour.
newsitem.headline: Beepers go awry across U.S. for half-hour.

text.p: Some 100,000 pagers rang wild across America on Thursday, rousing a slumbering West Coast and making New York commuters wonder if "Road Runner," the beeping cartoon character, had boarded their bus.

The half-hour beeping spree that made some offices sound like a gerbil's convention was caused by a single wrong number punched into a computer system, a spokeswoman for the pager company SkyTel said.

SkyTel, operated by the Mobile Telecommunication Technologies Corp., said an estimated 100,000 of its customers received between 20 and 25 erroneous beeps from about 8:16 a.m. EST to 8:42 a.m. and then more wrong numbers for five minutes later in the morning.

Some SkyTel users reported the beeps coming with even greater frequency and one New York commuter said the woman next to him on the bus headed for Wall Street was so impressed with the constant beeping that she declared, "Boy, you are a busy man."
SkyTel pagers transmit written and numeric messages plus news headlines.

Spokeswoman Ann Marie Potts said a new customer was mistakenly given a code used by SkyTel to send news headlines as a personal pin number. When that pin number was activated it went to all the customers of the headline service, triggering beeps and messages across the country.

In turn, customers began phoning the numbers on their pager screens, thus reactivating the pin number and generating even more messages. The pin number was taken off line but when engineers tried to restore the headline service, Potts said, more erroneous messages were broadcast for about five minutes.
Many SkyTel users on the West coast were awakened before dawn by a stream of pages. Some said they arrived in bursts of a few seconds over a one-hour period.

David Coursey, a San Mateo, California-based journalist who covers high technology, said when he checked his pager it was stuffed with about 15 messages that had arrived in two batches early in the morning.
"Fortunately it was on vibrate mode, but I was amazed when I got up," he said. "I was looking at it, and I was thinking, did Bill Gates die?"
Ginny Nevins, who works for the computer firm NCR in Atlanta, said she was bombarded with numbers flashing across her pager. She was surprised when her own telephone number showed up.

"The phone went nuts. I've had people calling from all over the country," said Nevins, who is an executive assistant for project management at NCR. "I'm extremely frustrated. I don't want to turn my pager off because I need it. I can't ignore my phone, I depend on it."

An answering machine in the Baltimore area yielded the following recording: "Hi. No, I'm not paging you. There's something really crazy going on with the ... paging company. So please, please stop calling me. I'm so sorry about your pager going crazy and my pager going crazy and my phone line. Thank you very much."
Janet Sheppard, of Bound Brook, N.J., said she had about 50 messages on her answering machine when she got home from work in the early afternoon, then got 12 more calls in the next 45 minutes.

Most of the people with whom she spoke directly "have been pleasant" she said. "But some of the answering machine messages have been pretty rude." Said one caller to the answering machine: "If you're going to page me the least you can do is answer your phone"
As a result of the mixup, and the fact that her phone number had been posted on the digital age equivalent of a telephone booth wall, Sheppard said she was going to change her number.
"Lots of people know how to get in touch with me now," she said with a laugh.
